title: Set Out and Plant a Deciduous Fruit Orchard

lessons.title: Preparing and marking out the orchard
lessons.html:
Planning comes first

A new orchard of apples, pears, peaches or plums will stand for 15 years or more. Mistakes made at planting are hard to fix later. The farm manager decides the cultivar, the rootstock, the spacing between rows and between trees, and the direction of the rows. Your job is to help mark out and plant correctly.

Soil preparation

Before planting, the soil is usually prepared months ahead. It may be ripped deep to break hard layers, lime and fertiliser are worked in according to soil tests, and ridges may be made where drainage is poor. Weeds are removed.

Setting out the rows

Setting out means marking exactly where each tree will go, so rows are straight and spacing is the same.

  1. Mark a straight base line along one side of the block using pegs and a long string or wire.
  2. Make a second line at a right angle to the base line. A simple way is the 3-4-5 method: measure 3 m along one line and 4 m along the other; when the distance between the two points is exactly 5 m, the corner is square.
  3. Measure the row spacing along the base line and put a peg for each row.
  4. Along each row, measure the tree spacing with a marked wire or tape and put a peg where each tree will be planted.
  5. Look down the rows from the end. Pegs should line up straight in every direction.

Tools you need

  • Measuring tape or marked wire
  • Pegs (wood or bamboo) and a hammer
  • String line
  • Spade, pick or auger for planting holes

Work carefully. A row that is out of line causes problems for tractors, sprayers and trellis wires for many years.

lessons.title: Planting the young trees
lessons.html:
Handling nursery trees

Young trees come from the nursery, often as bare-root trees in winter, when they are dormant. The roots must never dry out. Keep the trees in the shade, with roots covered with wet sacking or damp soil, until you plant them. Do not leave them on the back of a bakkie in the sun or wind.

Planting steps

  1. Dig a hole at the peg, wide and deep enough for the roots to spread out without bending.
  2. Cut off broken or damaged roots cleanly with sharp secateurs, as your supervisor shows you.
  3. Place the tree in the hole at the same depth it grew in the nursery.
  4. Keep the graft union (the bump where the cultivar joins the rootstock) well above the soil, usually a hand-width. If it is buried, the cultivar can form its own roots and the rootstock benefit is lost.
  5. Check the tree is upright and in line with the row.
  6. Fill in with loose topsoil, shaking the tree gently so soil fills between the roots.
  7. Firm the soil with your foot to remove air pockets, but do not stamp hard.
  8. Water the tree well straight after planting, even if the soil looks damp.

After planting

  • Tie the tree to a stake or trellis wire with soft ties, not wire that cuts the bark.
  • Cut the tree back (heading back) to the height your supervisor gives you.
  • Paint the trunk with white tree paint if this is farm practice, to protect against sunburn.
  • Keep weeds away from the young tree and check irrigation drippers.

Records

Write down the block, cultivar, rootstock, number of trees planted and the date. Report any trees that were damaged or missing.

Key points

  • The manager decides cultivar, rootstock and spacing.
  • Use a base line, the 3-4-5 method and pegs to set out straight rows.
  • Never let tree roots dry out before planting.
  • Keep the graft union above the soil.
  • Firm the soil and water the tree straight after planting.
